title: Why is pooling virtual threads an anti-pattern (they're cheap — one-per-task is intended), and when you need to bound concurrency why use a Semaphore instead of a thread pool?
shortTitle: Why pooling virtual threads is an anti-pattern — Semaphore for bounded concurrency

s1_definition.profdef: Virtual threads are cheap (~1KB) and disposable — creating one per task via `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` is the intended model. Pooling them with `newFixedThreadPool(n, Thread.ofVirtual().factory())` reintroduces the bottleneck VTs were designed to remove: a fixed pool of N threads limiting concurrency to N. When you need to bound concurrency against a finite resource (DB pool of 100 connections, rate-limited API at 500 RPS), use a `Semaphore(100)` — it limits the WORK (how many tasks access the resource) without limiting the THREADS (millions of VTs can still exist, most just waiting on the semaphore).
s1_definition.analogy: Virtual threads = free disposable tokens. Pooling them = "only give out 100 tokens total" — defeats the purpose (tokens are free!). The real constraint is the number of bank tellers (DB connections). Use a semaphore = "only 100 customers can approach tellers at once; rest wait in line." Unlimited tokens, limited teller access.
s1_definition.oneliner: Don't pool VTs — they're cheap (one-per-task). Bound the RESOURCE (Semaphore), not the THREADS (pool). newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor + Semaphore(dbPoolSize).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Virtual threads are cheap (~1KB) and disposable — creating one per task via `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` is the intended model. Pooling them with `newFixedThreadPool(n, Thread.ofVirtual().factory())` reintroduces the bottleneck VTs were designed to remove: a fixed pool of N threads limiting concurrency to N. When you need to bound concurrency against a finite resource (DB pool of 100 connections, rate-limited API at 500 RPS), use a `Semaphore(100)` — it limits the WORK (how many tasks access the resource) without limiting the THREADS (millions of VTs can still exist, most just waiting on the semaphore).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Virtual threads = free disposable tokens. Pooling them = "only give out 100 tokens total" — defeats the purpose (tokens are free!). The real constraint is the number of bank tellers (DB connections). Use a semaphore = "only 100 customers can approach tellers at once; rest wait in line." Unlimited tokens, limited teller access.

**One line to remember:** Don't pool VTs — they're cheap (one-per-task). Bound the RESOURCE (Semaphore), not the THREADS (pool). newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor + Semaphore(dbPoolSize).

sections.s2_technical:
Pooling virtual threads is an anti-pattern. Thread pools exist to REUSE expensive platform threads, but virtual threads are cheap and disposable — you should create a new one per task with `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` and let it die when the task ends. Putting them in a fixed pool reintroduces the very queueing and limit that virtual threads were designed to eliminate.

If you genuinely need to LIMIT concurrency against a scarce resource (a database connection pool of 50, or an external API rate limit), the right tool is a `Semaphore`, not a bounded thread pool. Each task still runs on its own virtual thread but first acquires a permit: `semaphore.acquire(); try { callDb(); } finally { semaphore.release(); }`. This caps concurrent access without capping the number of virtual threads.

A banking example: 10,000 report requests each run on their own virtual thread, but a `Semaphore(50)` ensures no more than 50 hit the reporting database at once, matching its connection pool. Senior nuance: "unlimited virtual threads + Semaphore for the bottleneck" is the idiom; a fixed virtual-thread pool is almost always wrong because it limits cheap threads instead of the expensive resource.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — A team wrapped virtual threads in a fixed pool of 50 to "limit load", which queued tasks and wasted the cheap-thread advantage while still hammering the database. Fix: create one virtual thread per task and use a `Semaphore(50)` to cap concurrent database access, limiting the scarce resource instead of the free threads.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Input: 100 report tasks, each needing a scarce DB connection.

**Step 2.** Every task gets its OWN virtual thread — no pool, no reuse, no queueing of cheap threads.

**Step 3.** Before touching the DB each task calls `semaphore.acquire()`; only 5 permits exist, so at most 5 run the DB section at once.

**Step 4.** The permit is released in a `finally`, letting the next waiting virtual thread proceed.

**Step 5.** Peak concurrent DB access never exceeds 5, while all 100 tasks still run on their own virtual threads.

```text
INFO: peak DB concurrency = 5 (Semaphore, not a thread pool)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ❌ ANTI-PATTERN: pool VTs
    FixedThreadPool(100, VT factory) → only 100 VTs → bottleneck!

  ✅ CORRECT: VT per task + Semaphore
    newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() → 100,000 VTs
    Semaphore(100) → only 100 access DB at once
    99,900 VTs wait on semaphore (blocking = cheap for VTs!)
    DB never overwhelmed. All tasks eventually complete.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Pooling virtual threads is an anti-pattern because VTs are cheap and disposable — the pool reintroduces the exact bottleneck they were designed to remove. Use `newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` for unlimited VTs, then gate finite resources with `Semaphore(n)`. The Semaphore limits how many tasks ACCESS the resource (DB connections, API rate limits) without limiting how many THREADS exist. 100K virtual threads with Semaphore(100) = all tasks eventually complete, only 100 hit the DB at any time.
